MattBlissett · Oct 31, 2026

15+ years of expectations around how a website can be run were upended by scrapers for LLM training.

They ignore robots.txt rules and seem to scrape as quickly and as broadly as possible. Unlike search engines, it doesn't matter to the LLM provider if the website is offline. Unlike search engines, they take steps to be anonymous and difficult to block, including using residential proxy services and other shared IP space.

I try and keep an open data repository online, but it was not designed for this. Cloudflare is hopefully a temporary fix while we redesign backend and frontend components.

The end result is going to be worse for users — slower querying, less flexibility as we primarily expose what we can precalculate, shifting CPU and bandwidth load to the user's device rather than our servers.

haukebri · Oct 31, 2026

I'm on the other side of this: my job is driving a real browser through websites to test them, so I'm usually the thing Cloudflare is trying to spot.

What decides whether it works for me isn't the challenge solver, it's the browser. Headless gets flagged within a request or two on a CF-protected site. A real Chrome with a persistent profile and a normal pace keeps going for weeks, until they tighten a rule and it dies halfway through a test run.

The thing that actually got me out of it was to stop fighting the front door. Most of the teams I work with can hand over a staging host behind basic auth, or a test account on an allowlist. Then Turnstile isn't in the path at all and the test measures their app instead of my evasion skills.

Where there's no staging I keep a saved human session and reuse the cookies instead of solving anything. Slower, but it survives most rollouts. (Until it doesn't, and then I'm re-authenticating by hand at 9am.)
